1. Frontend vs Backend: What's the difference?

Every website can have two major parts:

Frontend

The visible portion: design, text, images, buttons and layout.

Backend

The server-side portion: processing requests, managing data and handling private operations.

Frontend: What people see

Imagine a professor from Australia opens your portfolio website.

They can see your name, photo, research interests, publications, educational qualifications, and CV download button.

All these are part of the frontend.

The three fundamental frontend technologies are:

Technology

Purpose

Example

HTML

Website structure

Your name and biography

CSS

Website appearance

Fonts, colors, spacing

JavaScript

Website interactions

Mobile menus, filters

Backend: What happens behind the scenes

Suppose you want to add a feature where visitors can send you messages through your website.

When someone submits a message, the backend might receive it, validate the information, store it in a database, and send you an email.

Backend technologies include Python, Node.js, PHP, and Java.

Important: Your portfolio website might not need a backend at all. A simple portfolio containing information, publications, photographs, and CV links can work as a static website.

3. The easiest way to edit your ChatGPT website

I checked OpenAI's official instructions. You can edit a ChatGPT Site without learning programming first.

  1. Open ChatGPT on your computer.

  2. Find Sites in the sidebar, or open the original conversation where you built the site.

  3. Select your portfolio and click the edit icon.

  4. Describe your changes in normal English, such as “Add my latest conference publications and redesign the research section.”

  5. Review the website preview.

  6. Click Publish to update the live website.

You may also see an Edit site option directly on the published website while signed in as its owner.

OpenAI Help Center

4. How websites are built and published

Frontend

HTML • CSS • JavaScript • React

Backend (optional)

Python • Node.js • APIs

Database (optional)

Supabase • PostgreSQL • Firebase

Hosting: Vercel / GitHub Pages / ChatGPT Sites

Hosting makes your website accessible on the internet. Not every website needs all three layers.

For your personal portfolio, I would initially focus on learning frontend development, followed by GitHub and Vercel for publishing. You can explore backend development later when you want features such as an admin dashboard, publication management system, or visitor accounts.

Your web development learning roadmap

8-week beginner roadmap

Suggested pace

Approximately 1–2 hours of practice per day. The timeline is flexible.

  1. Week 1 — HTML

    Understand website structure and build your first academic profile page.

  2. Week 2 — CSS

    Learn colors, layouts, fonts, responsiveness, and professional website design.

  3. Week 3 — JavaScript

    Make buttons, menus, publication filters, and other interactive features work.

  4. Week 4 — Git and GitHub

    Learn to save versions of your code, organize projects, and restore earlier changes.

  5. Week 5 — React

    Learn to build reusable sections and manage website content more efficiently.

  6. Week 6 — Backend basics

    Learn APIs, servers, databases, and how a website can handle information securely.

  7. Week 7 — Deployment

    Publish your portfolio through Vercel, connect GitHub, and optionally configure a custom domain.

  8. Week 8 — Final project

    Complete your portfolio, optimize it for mobile, and learn how to maintain it independently.

Lesson 1: Build your first webpage

We're going to create a very simple version of your portfolio.

Step 1 — Create a folder

On your computer:

  1. Open your Desktop.

  2. Create a new folder called My-Portfolio.

  3. Open VS Code.

  4. Click File → Open Folder and select My-Portfolio.

  5. Create a new file inside it named index.html.

Your project should look like this:

My-Portfolio

index.html

Step 2 — Write your first code

Copy this code and paste it inside index.html.

HTML

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <title>Pamel Das | Portfolio</title>
</head>
<body>

    <h1>Pamel Das</h1>

    <h2>Electrical Engineer & Researcher</h2>

    <p>
        Welcome to my personal portfolio.
        I am interested in biomedical signal
        processing, artificial intelligence,
        and electrical engineering.
    </p>

    <h2>Education</h2>
    <p>
        Chittagong University of
        Engineering & Technology (CUET)
    </p>

    <h2>Research Interests</h2>
    <ul>
        <li>Biomedical Signal Processing</li>
        <li>Artificial Intelligence</li>
        <li>Brain-Computer Interfaces</li>
        <li>Machine Learning</li>
    </ul>

    <button onclick="alert('Welcome to my website!')">
        Click Me
    </button>

</body>
</html>

Step 3 — Run your website

Save the file by pressing Ctrl + S.

Then open the My-Portfolio folder and double-click index.html. It should open in your default web browser.

Your first website will look approximately like this:

file:///.../My-Portfolio/index.html

Pamel Das

Electrical Engineer & Researcher

Welcome to my personal portfolio. I am interested in biomedical signal processing, artificial intelligence, and electrical engineering.

Education

Chittagong University of Engineering & Technology (CUET)

Research Interests

• Biomedical Signal Processing • Artificial Intelligence • Brain-Computer Interfaces • Machine Learning

The preview above illustrates the page structure. The actual browser will use default HTML styling.

2. Understand what you just wrote

Code

Meaning

<html>

Beginning of the webpage

<head>

Information about the webpage

<title>

Text shown on the browser tab

<body>

Visible webpage content

<h1>

Main heading

<h2>

Secondary heading

<p>

Paragraph

<ul> and <li>

A list and its items

<button>

Creates a clickable button

The button in this example uses a small amount of JavaScript through onclick. We'll learn how that works in a later lesson.

Practical Task 2: Customize your homepage heading

We'll make your name stand out using CSS.

Step 1 — Open style.css

Scroll to the bottom of the file and add:

CSS
h1 {
    font-size: 52px;
    font-weight: 800;
    color: #1764cc;
    letter-spacing: -1.5px;
}

Step 2 — Save and see the changes

Press Ctrl + S, return to your browser, and refresh with Ctrl + R.

Your main heading should now appear larger, bolder, and blue.

Step 3 — Experiment with the design

Try changing:

CSS
font-size: 52px;

to:

CSS
font-size: 64px;

Refresh the browser again and observe the difference.

What you're learning by doing: font-size controls text size, font-weight controls thickness, color controls text color, and letter-spacing controls spacing between characters.

One important detail: if your website already has a more specific CSS rule for the heading, that rule may override the new h1 rule. We'll inspect that if the appearance doesn't change.
